# Differences from the originals

Where BlitzLLVM can not behave like Blitz3D or BlitzPlus, because the system they were made for is gone, this is how it behaves instead.

## Multiplayer

The multiplayer commands (`StartNetGame`, `HostNetGame`, `JoinNetGame`, `StopNetGame`, `CreateNetPlayer`, `DeleteNetPlayer`, `SendNetMsg`, `RecvNetMsg` and the rest) used DirectPlay in the originals, which is no longer available. In BlitzLLVM the programs that join a game connect to the program that hosts it over TCP, on port 40500. The host passes messages on to the other programs.

* Games made with BlitzLLVM can only play with other games made with BlitzLLVM. They can not join, or be joined by, a program made with Blitz3D.
* The port can be changed with the environment variable `BLITZ_NETGAME_PORT`. Every program of a game has to use the same one, and the host needs it to be open in its firewall.
* `StartNetGame` shows a dialog that asks whether to host or to join. When joining, the address of the host is asked on the console.
* The environment variable `BLITZ_DIALOG_ANSWER` presses a button of a dialog without showing it (0 is the first button), which is meant for automated runs.

## Network addresses

`CountHostIPs` looks up a host and remembers its addresses for `HostIP`. An empty name is this computer, which has one address for every network interface that is up, with the loopback address (127.0.0.1) last. `UDPStreamIP` is the first of those. Only IPv4 addresses are returned.

## Mip maps

Textures with flag 8 get a chain of mip maps and are sampled with trilinear filtering, which blends between two levels. The levels are made by averaging 2 by 2 texels, so masked (flag 4) and alpha textures average their alpha as well, which is also what the original did and makes their edges soft from afar. The levels of a texture that is drawn on (`TextureBuffer`) are made again before the texture is next used in a scene. The levels that are stored in a block compressed DDS file are used instead of made ones. A texture with frames (`LoadAnimTexture`, `CreateTexture` with frames) is one sheet, so its smallest levels blend the frames that are next to each other. There is no anisotropic filtering.

## Samplers

`CreateSampler`, `SetTextureSampler` and the `SetSampler...` commands are an extension. A sampler holds how a texture is read, and one sampler can be set on many textures. Without a sampler a texture is read with what its flags say. The modes are numbers:

| Setting | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Filters (`SetSamplerFilterMin`, `Mag`, `Mip`) | Nearest | Linear | | |
| Address modes (`SetSamplerAddressModeU`, `V`, `W`) | Repeat | Mirror | Clamp | Border (`SetSamplerBorderColor`, opaque black by default) |

`SetSamplerAnisotropy` takes 1 (off) or more and is kept inside the limit of the graphics card, which is also what happens to `SetSamplerLodBias`. `SetSamplerLodMin` and `SetSamplerLodMax` count mip levels from level 0. A sampler does not make mip levels (flag 8 does, see Mip maps above). Every setting can be read back with the `GetSampler...` commands (`GetSamplerAnisotropy`, `GetSamplerBorderColorR` to `A` and so on), which return what the sampler keeps. Without the `VK_EXT_custom_border_color` extension a border color is read as the closest of transparent black, opaque black and opaque white. `FreeSampler` sends the textures that use the sampler back to the settings of their flags.

## Depth buffer

The depth buffer is reversed and a 32-bit float: the near plane of `CameraRange` is written as 1 and the far plane as 0, and the closer surface wins. Blitz3D used a 16 or 24-bit buffer that is 0 at the near plane, which spends most of its precision close to the camera and makes far surfaces flicker through each other (z-fighting). With the reversed float buffer the precision is almost even over the whole range, so distant surfaces that are close together stay apart without having to push `near` out. This changes nothing a program can see except that z-fighting is much rarer. The depth is still not linear in the buffer itself (it is `near / distance` for a perspective camera, and linear for `CameraProjMode 2`), but the buffer is never read back by a program: `ProjectedZ` is the distance in front of the camera, and `Graphics3D`'s depth argument is not used.

## Console window on Windows

Programs are built for the GUI subsystem, so starting one (by double click, or from a window of the program) does not open a console window next to its own window. If the program is started from a terminal, it uses that terminal: `Print`, `Write`, `Input`, `DebugLog` and runtime errors work as on other systems, and they follow the redirection of the terminal (`program.exe > out.txt` writes `Print` to the file, `2> log.txt` writes `DebugLog`). Started without a terminal there is nothing to print to, so `Print` and `DebugLog` show nothing (`DebugLog` still goes to an attached debugger), and a runtime error is shown in a message box. The terminal does not wait for a GUI program, so its prompt may appear before the output of the program ends; use `start /wait program.exe` to wait. A program that runs `blitzcc` without `-o` runs from `blitzcc`'s terminal, so its output is shown as usual.

For a program that never opens a window, build it with `blitzcc --console`, which creates a console program that opens a console window when started without a terminal. This is only done for Windows, other systems always have the console they were started from.

## 3D Studio models

`LoadMesh` and `LoadAnimMesh` also read `.3ds` files of 3D Studio (an extension: the original names them but its loader never got them to work with animations). `LoadMesh` makes one mesh of all the objects as they are at the first frame, and `LoadAnimMesh` makes a pivot with an entity for each object, light and camera, with the hierarchy and the animation of the file. The file type is told by what is in the file, not by its name.

* 3D Studio is right-handed with z up, so y and z are swapped and the corners of every triangle are put in the order that Blitz3D calls the front. `LoaderMatrix` does not change this.
* Normals are made from the smoothing groups of the faces: faces that share a group and a vertex share a normal, and a face without a group is flat. The pictures of 3D Studio start at the bottom, so v is flipped. There is one set of texture coordinates.
* Materials become brushes: the diffuse color, the shininess, the transparency (as the alpha of the brush), two sided (`EntityFX` 16), additive (blend 3), flat shading (`EntityFX` 4) and a self-illumination of more than half (`EntityFX` 1, full bright). The first texture map is the texture of the brush, with its tiling, offset and rotation applied to the coordinates of the vertices, and clamped if the map says it is not tiled. The names are looked for next to the model, and then in the folder of the program. Other maps (bump, specular, reflection, opacity) and the ambient and specular colors are not used.
* Keys become the frames of an animation at 30 frames a second. The rotations are added up from key to key as the file stores them, and the frames of the file are used as they are. The curves of the keys (tension, continuity, bias) are not used, the animation goes straight from key to key.
* Lights are `LIGHT` entities (point, or spot lights with their hotspot and falloff angles as the cone, a range from the outer attenuation, and the color times the multiplier) and are hidden if they are off. Cameras are pivots, as the camera of a model is not one to render with. Both are turned to look at their target, also while the target moves. The color of a light over time, the field of view and the morphs and visibility keys of objects are not used.
* A node that the file marks as hidden is a hidden entity, and is not in the mesh of `LoadMesh`. A dummy object is a pivot with the name of its instance.

## Stop

`Stop` is a breakpoint for a debugger. In a debug build (`-d`) it is a breakpoint instruction (`llvm.debugtrap`), which stops in an attached debugger and ends the program with a signal when there is none. In any other build it does nothing.

## AppTitle

The second argument of `AppTitle` is asked when somebody closes the window. If they cancel, the program carries on; otherwise the window closes as it would have without the question.

## SystemProperty

| Property | Windows | Elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `appdir` | The folder of the program. | The folder of the program. |
| `tempdir` | `%TEMP%` | `$TEMP`, `$TMPDIR` or `/tmp`. |
| `windowsdir` | `%SystemRoot%` | `/etc/` (`/System/` on macOS), where the system keeps its settings. |
| `systemdir` | The System32 folder. | `/usr/lib/` (`/System/Library/` on macOS), where the system keeps its libraries. |

Folders end with a separator, except for the ones of Windows, which are as the system gives them.

## Colors

The 3D commands that take a color (`EntityColor`, `BrushColor`, `VertexColor`, `LightColor`, `AmbientLight`, `CameraClsColor`, `CameraFogColor`, `BSPAmbientLight` and the color of `LightMesh`) take floats from 0 to 255, so programs that pass whole numbers work as before. Vertex colors are stored as 16-bit floats (also on the GPU) and not as one byte per part, so `VertexColor` followed by `VertexRed`, `VertexGreen`, `VertexBlue` and `VertexAlpha` returns what was set (limited to 0 to 255, and 0 to 1 for alpha) to within about 0.1 of the 0 to 255 scale and `LightMesh` adds light without rounding the colors in between. The 2D commands (`Color`, `ClsColor`, `GetColor` and `ColorRed`, `ColorGreen`, `ColorBlue`) work on pixels and stay whole numbers.

## Sound resampling

The original played sounds through FMOD, which brings them to the rate of the sound device with linear interpolation. That leaves mirror images of the sound above its own bandwidth, which makes sounds with a low rate (11025 Hz files like the rain of Stranded II) bright and crisp, and takes a little off the top of the rest. SDL_mixer resamples cleanly, so the same files sound duller. Set the environment variable `BLITZ_AUDIO_CLASSIC` (to anything) before the program starts to do what the original did. Pitch and looping are the same either way.

## Displays

The originals only know the main display: `CountGfxModes` and the other `GfxMode` commands list its modes, and `Graphics` always opens on it. BlitzLLVM adds commands for every connected display (`CountDisplays`, `PrimaryDisplay`, `DisplayName`, `DisplayX`, `DisplayY`, `DisplayWidth`, `DisplayHeight`, `DisplayDepth`, `DisplayRefreshRate`, `DisplayScale`), for the modes each one supports (`CountDisplayModes`, `DisplayModeWidth`, `DisplayModeHeight`, `DisplayModeDepth`, `DisplayModeRefreshRate`) and for the refresh rates of a size (`CountRefreshRates`, `RefreshRateAt`).

* Displays and modes are numbered from 1, like the modes of `GfxModeWidth`. A number that does not exist gives 0 (or an empty text for `DisplayName`) instead of stopping the program, because a display can be unplugged while the program runs. `CountDisplays` looks at the displays again each time it is called.
* The mode lists have every combination of size, depth and refresh rate once, from the smallest width to the largest, and always include the mode the display is in now. Refresh rates are rounded to whole Hz, and a display that does not tell its rate is taken to have 60 Hz.
* The commands can be asked before `Graphics` opens a window. When no display driver is available there is one display called "Default" with the sizes `CountGfxModes` gives.
* `Graphics` can not be told which display to open on yet; it opens on the main display.

## Microseconds and UInt64

`Microseconds` is the first command that returns a `UInt64` (an unsigned 64-bit integer), which the originals do not have. It counts the microseconds on the same clock as `MilliSecs`, but without the wrap around of the 31 bits that `MilliSecs` keeps, so `Microseconds() / 1000` is about `MilliSecs()` before that wrap. A 32-bit `Int` would overflow after 35 minutes, and a `Float` (24 bits of precision) stops counting single microseconds after 16 seconds.

* Keep the result in a variable declared with `:UInt64` (for example `start:UInt64 = Microseconds()`). A variable with no type or with `%` is an `Int`, which keeps only the lowest 32 bits and may come out negative; `#` is a `Float`, which rounds.
* `Str` and `Print` write all digits, and an expression with a `UInt64` and an `Int` is calculated as a `UInt64`, so `Microseconds() - start` is the elapsed time. Comparisons are unsigned, and `Int()` and `Float()` convert the value (the `Int` loses the upper bits).
* The start of the count is not fixed, like `MilliSecs`: only differences between two calls mean something. The clock is the system clock, so it can jump when the time is set.

## Types everywhere

The originals only have `Int`, `Float` and `String` (and custom types). BlitzLLVM adds `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `Long`, `ULong`, `Half` and `Double`, and every one of them, as well as `String` and custom types, works as a `Global`, a `Local`, a parameter (with default values), a return type, a field of a `Type`, a `Const` and the type of a `Dim` array. Types are written in the short form with a sign after the name (`%` Int, `%%` Long, `#` Float, `##` Double, `$` String, `.Name` custom type) or in the long form with `:Type` (`Count:UInt`, `Function Now:ULong()`). Whole numbers wrap around at the size of their type, so a `UByte` that is 255 and gets 1 added is 0, and `ULong` and `UInt` are never negative. `tests/suite/language_types.bb` checks the combinations.

The tables of built-in functions in the compiler can use the same types for parameters and return values (`b B h H i I l u x f d s`), not just `i f s`.

## Userlib declarations

A `.decls` file takes the same two ways to write a type as the language, for the parameters and the return type of a function, and they can be mixed in one file: `Scale#(value#, factor#)` is the same as `Scale:Float(value:Float, factor:Float)`. The long form is available for every type: `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `Int`, `UInt`, `Long`, `ULong`, `Half`, `Float`, `Double` and `String` (the names of the language, not case sensitive), plus `Pointer` for a bank or object parameter (`memory*` is the short form) and `Void` for a function that returns nothing (the default). Pointers can not be returned. The short form has `%`, `%%`, `#`, `##`, `$` and `*`, and a name without a type is still an `Int`. A decorated name after the closing bracket (`:"_Name@8"`) still works, and the `:` there is not confused with the one of a type, because a type comes before the bracket.

The original only had `Int`, `Float` and `String`. Numbers are passed as C types of the same size (`int8_t`, `uint16_t`, `int64_t`, `double`, ...); numbers smaller than 32 bits are sign extended or zero extended by the caller, like C compilers do. `Half` is passed as a half precision float (`_Float16`), which no test covers. `blitzcc +k` lists the types as they are written in the short form where there is one (`Scale# ( value#,factor# )`, `Big%% ( value%% )`), and in the long form for the others (`Now:ULong ( )`).
